sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV — high confidence; thresholds confirmed on LSLBC + statute, Sep 2026)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; thresholds confirmed on LSLBC + statute, Sep 2026
sections.markdown: Louisiana has a **real two-tier state regime under one board — the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors (LSLBC), La. R.S. 37:2150 et seq.** (1) A **state Residential license** is required for residential construction with a **project value of $50,000 or more**, and (2) a separate **Home Improvement** credential covers repair/improvement work on existing homes from **$7,500 up to $50,000**. Both numbers are confirmed on the regulator's own page — LSLBC "Types of Licenses": "Residential Construction exceeding $50,000 (including labor and materials)"; "Home improvement" = work on a preexisting residential structure "for which the project value is seven thousand five hundred dollars or more" (https://lslbc.gov/types-of-licenses/) — and in the statute's definitions, La. R.S. 37:2150.1 (home improvement contractor: project value "at least seven thousand five hundred dollars but less than fifty thousand dollars"; residential contractor: "fifty thousand dollars or more"; history through Acts 2025, No. 422; https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-37/rs-37-2150-1/). The LSLBC FAQ uses the same band: "exceeds $7,500 but not exceeding $50,000, a home improvement registration is required" (https://lslbc.gov/faq/). (Naming note: the FAQ calls it a "registration," the Types-of-Licenses page lists it as a license type — use "Home Improvement registration (LSLBC)" on the page and link the board.) Work **under $7,500 needs no state credential.** So a chimney reline or masonry rebuild in the $7.5k–$50k band needs at least the Home Improvement credential; a sweep or small repair is exempt. Unlike Alabama's municipal model (labeled comparison), this credential is **statewide.** Insurance: the LSLBC FAQ lists general liability (minimum $100,000) and workers' compensation proof before licensure. Public lookup: **lslbc.gov** (Verify a Contractor).

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: The LSLBC credential attests **financial responsibility, insurance, and a business-and-law component — not flue diagnosis or masonry skill.** (Exactly which exams the Home Improvement tier requires is not spelled out on the pages checked; the FAQ references an exam/administrative fee "for each classification and for Business and Law" — do not publish a "no exam" claim.) No LSLBC exam tests whether the holder can read a cracked liner. And everything **below $7,500 is uncredentialed** — the band where most sweeps and small repairs live. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) remain the competence signal.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV/DOC — high; mandatory form + a distinctive civil-law backstop)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: high; mandatory form + a distinctive civil-law backstop
sections.markdown: Louisiana **mandates seller disclosure** (contrast: Alabama has none). Under **La. R.S. 9:3196 et seq.**, covering property of one to four residential dwelling units, the seller **must** give the buyer the **Property Disclosure Document** (form prescribed by the Louisiana Real Estate Commission), disclosing **"known defects"** on an actual-knowledge basis. The **current LREC form — "Residential Property Disclosure Document (01/2026)," mandatory on and after January 1, 2026** (https://lrec.gov/blog/2026-mandatory-forms-now-online; form PDF linked from that LREC post: https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6696cedcb19f4a286c91f2e8/690a620785f143dee3fb608e_251020%20FILLABLE_%202026%20Property%20Disclosure%20Document%20(Final).pdf) — **asks in Section 5, item 22: "Are you aware of any defects with the fireplace(s)?"** and in item 24 asks whether the home has a smoke detector (10-yr lithium battery) and a **CO detector (long-life, sealed battery)**, footnoting La. R.S. 40:1581. The words **"chimney" and "flue" do not appear on the form** — chimney defects ride under the fireplace question. Louisiana's **distinctive extra lever is redhibition**: under **La. Civ. Code art. 2520**, a seller warrants against **redhibitory (hidden) defects** existing at delivery — a buyer can win **rescission of the sale or a price reduction** for a latent defect a reasonably prudent buyer wouldn't have found. Redhibition can be waived by clear "as-is" language, but it's a **civil-law remedy no common-law state offers.** No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: **The Louisiana Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law (La. R.S. 51:1401 et seq.)** gives a private right of action; under **R.S. 51:1409**, "If the court finds the unfair or deceptive method, act, or practice was knowingly used, after being put on notice by the attorney general, the court shall award three times the actual damages sustained," and attorney fees and costs are awarded when damages are — but the action is subject to a **"liberative prescription of one year running from the time of the transaction or act"** (https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-51/rs-51-1409/). The AG's Consumer Protection Section enforces and can seek injunctions. **3-business-day right to cancel a home-solicitation sale:** **La. R.S. 9:3538** — "the consumer has the right to cancel a home solicitation sale until midnight of the third business day after the day on which the consumer signs an agreement" (https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-9/rs-9-3538/); **R.S. 9:2711.1** extends the same right to **noncredit** home-solicitation sales by incorporating R.S. 9:3538–3541 (https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-9/rs-9-2711-1/). **Emergency trap:** under 9:3538 the consumer may not cancel if the consumer requested goods or services "without delay because of an emergency" and the seller has substantially performed — never sign an "emergency" authorization at the door. Redhibition stacks as a distinct sale-defect lever. Complaints: Louisiana AG Consumer Protection.

sections.rawHeading: 5 · Permits & codes (GOV/DOC — high; statewide code is a post-Katrina feature)
sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.confidenceNote: high; statewide code is a post-Katrina feature
sections.markdown: Louisiana has a **mandatory statewide code — the Louisiana State Uniform Construction Code (LSUCC), La. R.S. 40:1730.22 et seq.**, adopting the I-codes by reference (**§ 40:1730.28**) (contrast: Alabama's patchwork). This was a **post-Katrina reform** (Acts 2005, 1st Ex. Sess., No. 12) — the code exists statewide because of the 2005 hurricanes. **Editions in force (Sep 2026): 2021 IBC, IRC, IMC and IFGC with Louisiana amendments, effective January 1, 2023; the 2024 ICC editions are scheduled to take effect January 1, 2027** (LSUCC Council, https://lsuccc.la/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/LSUCCC_Louisiana-Construction-Code-Information.pdf). Page copy must anticipate the Jan 2027 flip. Chimney relines, rebuilds, crowns, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally **permit work** where a local building department administers the code; routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not (LOCAL practice varies).

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — high confidence; CORRECTED Sep 2026)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **Louisiana DOES have a statewide point-of-sale/lease CO-detector statute — La. R.S. 40:1581.** "All existing one- or two-family dwellings at the time of sale or lease shall contain, at a minimum, an operable carbon monoxide detector with a long-life, sealed battery," and likewise an operable ten-year sealed lithium-battery smoke detector (history: Acts 1991, No. 701; Acts 2009, No. 163; **Acts 2022, No. 458**) (https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=97690; https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1581/). The statute also reaches professional home-generator installations. It has soft teeth: noncompliance **is not a reason to deny an insurance claim, cannot delay the transfer, and creates no liability for real estate agents.** The 2026 LREC disclosure form asks the seller to state whether the CO detector is present. New construction additionally follows LSUCC/IRC R315. No inspection or certificate is required at sale — it is a self-reported requirement.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime located. **Chimney/wood-heat density is genuinely low in south Louisiana** (New Orleans, Acadiana — mild, humid, little heating demand) and **higher in north Louisiana** (Shreveport/Monroe uplands). Be honest on the page: much of the state is a light hearth market, and the statewide LSUCC is a **post-Katrina, storm-driven feature**, not a wood-heat one.

sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: Louisiana's dominant fraud pattern is **post-hurricane contractor and repair fraud**; the AG's Consumer Protection Section and the LSLBC pursue unlicensed and out-of-state "storm chaser" contractors, and the door-knock "we noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook R.S. 9:3538 home-solicitation + LUTPA matter. **Specific LA chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT YET CONFIRMED — name no companies.**

sections.title: Season calendar
sections.markdown: Humid subtropical; short, mild winters (shorter still on the Gulf/New Orleans belt, slightly longer in north LA). Burn season ~Dec–Feb. Rush: OCT–DEC. Best booking: MAR–SEP.

sections.title: Price seeding (internal)
sections.markdown: New Orleans metro runs **near national**; Baton Rouge and north Louisiana (Shreveport/Monroe) **at or below national.** Thin hearth demand statewide keeps the market small — regionalize modestly downward off the national ranges. (REF/editorial — replace with local quotes.)

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: Louisiana **tests the license⇄disclosure inverse-correlation thesis harder than any neighbor.** It licenses **more** than Alabama (a real two-tier LSLBC regime: $7,500 home-improvement floor, $50,000 residential line) AND discloses more (a mandatory LREC form that asks about fireplace defects by name) AND, per a check this pass, requires a working CO detector at every sale or lease of a one- or two-family home (R.S. 40:1581). What keeps the correlation from breaking outright is that no axis is *strong*: the credential tests business/insurance, not flues, and switches off under $7,500; the disclosure is actual-knowledge-only; and the CO rule is self-reported with express no-consequence clauses. The **real Louisiana story is the civil-law wildcard.** Louisiana is the only state where a buyer gets **redhibition (Civ. Code art. 2520)**: a hidden-defect action that can **rescind the whole sale** for a latent flue defect. Add that the statewide building code exists **because of Katrina**, not wood heat, and Louisiana's page writes itself around two oddities — redhibition and a storm-born code — in a state where chimneys are genuinely scarce down south.

faq.q: What should I check before hiring a chimney company in Louisiana?
faq.a: State licensing: YES — LSLBC Residential license at project value ≥ $50,000 (La. R.S. 37:2150.1) + Home Improvement registration $7,500–<$50,000; no state credential < $7,500. Registration or credential: YES — statewide Home Improvement registration (LSLBC). Seller disclosure at sale: YES — mandatory Property Disclosure Document (R.S. 9:3196 et seq.); 01/2026 LREC form item 22 asks about fireplace defects (no "chimney" wording); + redhibition (Civ. Code art. 2520). Right to cancel a sale made at your home: YES (R.S. 9:3538; noncredit via 9:2711.1) — lost if buyer requests emergency work and seller substantially performs. Carbon monoxide alarm law: YES at sale/lease — R.S. 40:1581 (operable long-life sealed CO detector in 1–2-family dwellings; no certificate, doesn't delay transfer). Where to check a contractor: lslbc.gov. Then ask the eight questions below, get the inspection findings in writing with photos, and never sign for "emergency" work on the day of a door-knock.
